blocks.title: The Law of Cosines
teacherCues: Write the three standard forms on the board: a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos A, etc. Explain each term.
Ask: When can we NOT use the Law of Sines? (Answer: when we have SSS or SAS.)

discoveryHook.scenario: When you know all three sides of a triangle but no angles, the Law of Sines won't help. The Law of Cosines is like a general Pythagorean theorem—it works for any triangle, not just right triangles.

explanation: The [[kw:Law of Cosines]] relates the three sides of a triangle to the cosine of an angle:
Standard form (to find a side): $$a^2 = b^2 + c^2 - 2bc \cos A$$
Alternative form (to find an angle): $$\cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2bc}$$
Use it for [[imp:SSS]] (three sides) or [[imp:SAS]] (two sides and the included angle).

visuals.title: When to Use Law of Cosines

formulaCard.title: Law of Cosines (Standard)
notes: The side on the left is opposite the angle at the end.
If C = 90°, it becomes the Pythagorean theorem.

examples.title: A – Label and Write
examples.prompt: In triangle ABC, a = 8, b = 6, C = 60°. Write the correct Law of Cosines formula to find c.
steps: The sides are a, b and known angle C, so use the formula with c² on the left.

examples.title: B – Find an Angle (SSS)
examples.prompt: If you know all three sides, which form of the Law of Cosines do you use? Explain to a partner why.
examples.peerPrompt: Discuss: The standard form has a squared side on the left. If you want an angle, which version isolates the cosine?
steps: Use the alternative form: cos A = (b² + c² – a²) / (2bc).
This solves directly for the angle.

examples.title: C – Check if Acute or Obtuse
examples.prompt: If cos B is negative, what kind of angle is B?
steps: Cosine is negative for angles between 90° and 180°.
So angle B is obtuse (greater than 90°).

confusionCorner.title: Don't Mix Up the Sides
confusionCorner.body: In the formula a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos A, the side squared on the left is opposite the angle A. The other two sides (b and c) are multiplied and used with cos A.

questions.prompt: The Law of Cosines formula to find side a is a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos ___.
hints: The angle must be opposite side a.
Side a is opposite angle A.

questions.prompt: When you are given all three sides of a triangle, which form of the Law of Cosines do you use? (Write 'alternative')
hints: You need to solve for an angle.
The form with cosine alone on the left.

questions.prompt: If the Pythagorean theorem is a special case of the Law of Cosines when the angle is ___ degrees.
hints: a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos 90° yields a² = b² + c² because cos 90° = 0.
The angle is a right angle.

blocks.title: Solving SSS Triangles
teacherCues: Draw a triangle with three sides labeled, e.g., a=8, b=19, c=14. Ask: Which angle should we find first? (the one opposite the longest side, B).
Work out cos B = (a² + c² – b²)/(2ac) ≈ –0.4509. B ≈ 116.8°.

discoveryHook.scenario: Given three sides, you have all the measurements but no angles. The Law of Cosines helps you find the largest angle first, ensuring the others are acute.

explanation: For SSS: use the alternative form to find the largest angle first (opposite the longest side).
Then use the Law of Sines to find a second angle (ensuring it's acute if the largest is obtuse).
Finally, the third angle is 180° minus the sum of the first two.

formulaCard.title: Alternative Form
notes: b is the longest side, so B is the largest angle.
If cos B is negative, B is obtuse.

examples.title: A – Find Largest Angle
examples.prompt: Given a=8 ft, b=19 ft, c=14 ft. Find angle B.

examples.title: B – Then Use Law of Sines
examples.prompt: After finding B, find angle A using the Law of Sines.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain to a partner: Why is it safe to use the Law of Sines now? (Because we already know the triangle is valid and B is obtuse, so A must be acute.)
steps: Use sin A / a = sin B / b.

confusionCorner.title: Largest Angle First
confusionCorner.body: Always find the angle opposite the longest side first. If it is obtuse, the other two must be acute, avoiding the ambiguous case when using Law of Sines.

questions.prompt: In SSS, you should find the angle opposite the ___ side first.
hints: It's the largest angle.
The side with the greatest length.

questions.prompt: If cos B is negative, is angle B acute or obtuse? (Enter 'obtuse')
hints: Cosine negative means angle > 90°.
Cosine of 120° is negative.

questions.prompt: After finding two angles, the third angle is found by subtracting their sum from ___°.
hints: Sum of angles in a triangle is 180°.
Subtract the two known angles from 180°.

blocks.title: Solving SAS Triangles
teacherCues: Draw a triangle with two sides and the included angle, e.g., b=9, c=12, A=25°. Find a.
Use a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos A. Compute a ≈ 5.41. Then use Law of Sines to find angles.

discoveryHook.scenario: A softball field: you know two distances and the angle between them. The Law of Cosines gives the third side, completing the triangle.

explanation: For SAS: use the standard form of the Law of Cosines to find the third side.
Then use the Law of Sines to find an angle (preferably the smaller one to avoid ambiguity).
Finally, the third angle is 180° minus the sum of the other two.

rows.1: sin B = b·sin A / a ≈ 9·sin25°/5.41 ≈ 0.7034 → B ≈ 44.7° (acute chosen)

formulaCard.title: Standard Form for Side
notes: The side a is opposite the given angle A.
After finding a, use Law of Sines to find another angle.

examples.title: A – Find side a
examples.prompt: Given b=9 m, c=12 m, A=25°. Find side a.

examples.title: B – Find Angle B
examples.prompt: Now use the Law of Sines to find angle B.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain: Which two ratios do you set equal? Why is B acute?
steps: sin B / b = sin A / a → sin B = b·sin A / a = 9·sin25° / 5.41 ≈ 0.7034.
B₁ ≈ 44.7° (acute), B₂ ≈ 135.3° (but would make A+B > 180°, so discard).

confusionCorner.title: Avoiding the Ambiguous Case
confusionCorner.body: After finding the side, use the Law of Sines to find the smaller of the two remaining angles first. Check that the larger angle doesn't violate the sum of angles.

questions.prompt: In the SAS case, the first step is to find the ___ side using the Law of Cosines.
hints: You have two sides and need the one opposite the given angle.
That completes the three sides.

questions.prompt: After finding side a, which law do you use to find angle B? (Write 'Law of Sines')
hints: You now have a side and opposite angle pair (a and A).
With another side (b), you can find its opposite angle.

questions.prompt: When using Law of Sines after SAS, choose the ___ angle first to avoid ambiguity.
hints: The smaller angle is the one opposite the shorter side.
It will be acute, so no ambiguous case.

blocks.title: Real-Life Applications
teacherCues: Show the softball field diagram: pitcher's mound 43 ft from home, bases 60 ft apart, angle at home 45°. Find the distance from pitcher to first base.
Work through the Law of Cosines: h² = 43² + 60² – 2·43·60·cos45°.

discoveryHook.scenario: Softball field geometry: using the Law of Cosines, you can find distances on the field without leaving the dugout.

explanation: The Law of Cosines models many real-life problems where you know two sides and the included angle.
For example, in navigation, finding the distance or bearing after traveling two legs.
Sketch the situation, label known sides and angle, then apply the appropriate form of the Law of Cosines.

formulaCard.title: Law of Cosines Application
notes: f = distance from home to pitcher, p = home to 1st base.
Angle H is the angle between those two segments.

examples.title: A – Softball Problem
examples.prompt: Find the distance from the pitcher's mound to first base.
steps: Label triangle HPF: H = 45°, f = 43 ft, p = 60 ft.
Use the Law of Cosines to find h opposite H: h² = f² + p² – 2fp cos H.

examples.title: B – Ship Bearing
examples.prompt: A ship goes 60 mi N, then 80 mi, and finds it is 139 mi from start. Find the angle at B.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain how to use the alternative form to find angle B, given all three sides. Which side is opposite B?
steps: Sides: a = 80 mi, b = 139 mi, c = 60 mi.
B ≈ 166.1°. Then the bearing from B to C is N 13.9° W.

examples.title: C – Center fielder throw
examples.prompt: Center fielder is 240 ft from home plate. Bases are 60 ft apart, home to third is 60 ft at a right angle. Find distance from center fielder to third base.
steps: Form triangle: home, center, third. Distance home-center = 240 ft, home-third = 60 ft, angle between them = 90° (since center is straight out and third is to the left).

confusionCorner.title: Right Angle Shortcut
confusionCorner.body: If the included angle is 90°, the Law of Cosines reduces to the Pythagorean theorem because cos90° = 0. Use that shortcut when possible.

questions.prompt: In the softball example, the angle at home plate is ___° because the line to the pitcher bisects the 90° base paths.
hints: Half of a right angle.

questions.prompt: What distance does the Law of Cosines compute in the softball field problem? (pitcher to first, home to second, etc.)
hints: Look at the sides: f=43, p=60, H=45°.
The unknown side is from pitcher's mound to first base.
questions.feedbackIfWrong: It's the distance from pitcher to first base.

questions.prompt: If the included angle is 90°, the Law of Cosines becomes the ___ theorem.
hints: a² = b² + c² – 2bc cos90° yields a² = b² + c² because cos90° = 0.
That's the Pythagorean theorem.

blocks.title: Blueprint Aid – Heron's Area Formula
teacherCues: Write Heron's formula on the board: Area = √[s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)], where s = (a+b+c)/2.
Work through an example: a=43, b=53, c=72 → s=84, area ≈ 1131.89.

discoveryHook.scenario: Given only the three side lengths of a triangular garden, Heron's formula calculates the area without knowing any height or angle—perfect for irregular plots.

explanation: [[kw:Heron's Area Formula]] gives the area of a triangle when you know all three sides.
It is derived from the Law of Cosines.

formulaCard.title: Heron's Area Formula
notes: Works for any triangle, even with integer sides.

examples.title: A – Find semiperimeter
examples.prompt: For a=43 m, b=53 m, c=72 m, find s.

examples.title: B – Compute Area
examples.prompt: Now use Heron's formula to find the area.
examples.peerPrompt: Explain each step to your partner: subtract each side from s, multiply them all with s, then take the square root.

examples.title: C – Another Triangle
examples.prompt: Use Heron's formula for a=5 in, b=9 in, c=8 in. Compute area.

confusionCorner.title: Semiperimeter, Not Perimeter
confusionCorner.body: Don't forget to divide (a+b+c) by 2 to get s. Using the full perimeter will give a much larger (incorrect) area.

questions.prompt: In Heron's formula, s stands for ___ (half the perimeter).
hints: It's half of the sum of the sides.
The term starts with 'semi'.

questions.prompt: Compute s for a triangle with sides 6, 8, 10. (Enter a number)
hints: Add the sides: 6+8+10 = 24.
Divide by 2.

questions.prompt: Heron's formula uses a ___ root of the product s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c).
hints: The symbol is √.
It's the opposite of squaring.

challengeCorner.prompt: A triangle has sides 13, 14, 15. Using Heron's formula, find its area. (Hint: s=21, and the product s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c) = 21·8·7·6 = 7056. Square root of 7056 = 84.)
